Remote Tool Abuse 001 — a guided SOC investigation
  1 / 1
Start●

You have been handed an alert. Work out what happened.

no experience needed

This is the alert your security team woke up to. Read it before you touch anything:

The alertRemote support agent installed or registered as a service - on sec-win-05, a user signed in from an external address, three minutes later an application was installed, one minute after that the same application was running as SYSTEM with a service as its parent, a scheduled task was registered in the same second, and the server then began opening small, evenly spaced outbound connections to a named vendor relay endpoint.

Your job is to decide one thing: is this a real attack that must be escalated, or a false alarm that can be closed? You will answer it the way a real analyst does — not by guessing, but by following the evidence from the very first search to the last and writing down what you find as you go. By the final card you will know what was installed, by whom, how it was made to survive a reboot, and where it was phoning home.

What makes this one unusual

The payload here is not malware. It is a commercially sold remote-support product — the same category of software every help desk on earth uses to take control of a user's PC remotely. It is bought, licensed, and signed by a reputable publisher. Antivirus sees a signed binary installed by a user. An application allow-list may approve the vendor outright. There is no exploit and nothing that looks strange to any single control.

So the evidence is all in the sequence and the identity, not in the binary: who ran the installer, what privilege it ended up with sixty seconds later, whether something was registered to bring it back after a reboot, and where it connects. That is exactly what you will go and look at.

What this guide is

It starts at zeroNo security knowledge and no Elastic experience needed. The investigation itself is clicking and reading; the only typing is your report, at the end.
The pictures are realEvery screen picture in this guide is a photograph of the running lab, taken by screenshotting the real Kibana. Nothing is drawn from memory.
It never leaves you guessingAfter every step it says the exact number or text you should now be looking at, and it tells you what to write down.
It cleans up after itselfOne file starts the lab — setup-lab.cmd on Windows, setup-lab.sh on macOS or Linux — and one removes it completely. Nothing is left behind.

How to move around

This guide is a deck of cards, one step each. Move through it however you like:

  • The Next and Back buttons at the bottom, or the arrow keys on your keyboard.
  • The row of pills under the header jumps you straight to any step.
  • On a phone, swipe left and right.
  • Press ? any time for help, or the printer icon to save the whole guide as a PDF.
Two honest notes, and they are the good kind

1. The numbers in this guide are not predictions. The screen pictures are real screenshots of this lab, running Kibana 9.1.0, and every word, button, column name, row count and timestamp in them is what your own screen will show. They were read off those exact screens, and the setup file re-checks every one of them each time it builds the lab. If your screen and the picture disagree, stop and follow the If it breaks card near the end before you carry on.

2. From card 21 the guide hands you an answer. The timeline card prints all seven events assembled, and then a model paragraph you could paste straight into your report. That is deliberate, and it is here because a timeline is not something you are supposed to guess the shape of — it is a technique, and the only way to learn the technique is to see one that is already right.

So use it the way a navigator uses a map. The thing being assessed is the report you write: your reasoning, your evidence, your verdict. Copying a screenshot or pasting this paragraph is not investigating, it is the easiest way to fail. Write it in your own words, and fill in the last card's fields from your own screen — all of which stay blank until you do.

The one thing you need first

Docker Desktop, installed and running. That is the only prerequisite. The lab runs inside it and installs nothing else on your computer. If you do not have Docker Desktop yet, ask your instructor — this lab assumes it is already there.

Prep1

The words you need to know

read once

You do not have to memorise these. Read them once now; every card refers back to one of them, and you can come back to this card at any time.

The tools you are looking at

Elasticsearchthe database that stores and searches the logs. Answers on http://localhost:9200.
Kibanathe web interface on top of it, on http://localhost:5601. Every screen in this guide is Kibana.
Data viewa saved name for a family of indices. Ours are auth-* and network-*. Older builds call it an index pattern.
Discoverthe hunting screen: a query bar, a histogram and the matching records. We spend all our time here.
Mappingthe type of every field — IP, keyword, text, number. It decides how you are allowed to query a field.
Field statisticsthe second tab on a result set: how many documents a field covers, how many distinct values it has, and how they are spread.
Dev Toolsa Kibana console that takes requests written as JSON and shows the raw JSON reply.
Detection rulethe logic behind an alert. It runs your query on a schedule, every minute here. No rule means no alerts.

The subject of this lab

RMMRemote Monitoring and Management — legitimate software for letting support staff control a machine remotely. AnyDesk, TeamViewer, ScreenConnect, Atera and Splashtop are all in this category.
RMM abusean attacker installing one of those products on a machine they already control. The binary is genuine, so detection has to come from context, not from signatures.
Relaythese products rarely connect two machines directly; the traffic goes through the vendor's own cloud servers. So the outbound destination looks like a large, entirely legitimate SaaS provider.
Windows servicea program Windows starts at boot and runs whether or not anyone is logged in. A tool that becomes a service survives reboots and logoffs.
SYSTEMthe built-in account that owns services and the OS itself. If a program's user.name is SYSTEM, no person is using it.
Parent processwhat started a program, in process.parent.name. explorer.exe is the desktop — a person started it. services.exe is the service controller — it is a service.
Scheduled task (4698)Windows runs a program on a trigger. Event 4698 is written when a task is created — a strong signal, because somebody deliberately arranged for it to start again later.
Beaconinga program contacting its controller on a timer. The regularity is the give-away, not the volume.

Three words that decide your verdict

IOCIndicator of Compromise — a piece of evidence that something bad happened: an address, a domain, a program, a service name. The relay in this lab is an IOC.
True positivethe alert fired and something bad really did happen. Your job is to decide which one this is.
False positivethe alert fired and nothing bad happened. Close it, with a reason.
One trap to know about before you start

The fields in this lab are indexed as exact keywords, so the search box treats msbuild.exe and MSBuild.exe as two different values, and a path typed with the wrong capital as none at all. Copy values by pasting them, or by clicking them out of the results — never retype them from memory. A mistyped capital is the single most common reason a beginner gets zero results from a query that is actually correct.

Prep2

What is in the folder

read once

Everything below is run from inside the lab folder. Open a terminal and go there first, then list what is in it.

In your terminal, from the lab foldercd /path/to/rmm-tool-abuse-001 ls

You should see these. The first four are the only things you run; the rest is data and documentation.

FileWhat it is
setup-lab.cmdWindows. Builds the whole lab: Elasticsearch, Kibana, the data views and the detection rule.

teardown.cmdWindows. Removes everything the setup file created, and nothing else.
teardown.shmacOS / Linux. The same thing, in the same order.
auth.ndjsonThe account and process log data — logons, failed logons, logoffs, lockouts, scheduled-task registrations, process creations. 272 documents.
network.ndjsonThe network traffic log data — SMB, RPC, DNS, LDAP, HTTP/HTTPS, SSH, ICMP, with the named endpoint of each session. 148 documents.

network.jsonIndex template that fixes the field types for network-2026.09.22.

You never need to regenerate any of it

The log data was produced by a deterministic generator with a fixed seed, so it is byte-identical every time. If any of the five data files is missing, say so before you start rather than working around it.

Build3

Build the lab with one file

do now

This is the only step that needs Docker. Start Docker Desktop (Windows or macOS) or the Docker service (Linux) and wait until it says the engine is running.

Run one of these, from the lab folderWindows setup-lab.cmd macOS/Linux ./setup-lab.sh (once: chmod +x setup-lab.sh)

It takes two to five minutes the first time, because it downloads Elasticsearch and Kibana into containers. Every run after that is fast — the images are kept, only the containers restart.

The lines that matter are these. You should see all of them:

The last thing the setup file prints [verify] reading every walkthrough count back out of Elasticsearch every document in the auth data view = 272 every document in the network data view = 148 query 1 the scheduled task = 1 query 2 the installation on the server = 2 query 3 the external logon = 1 query 4 everything the server sent = 3 query 5 the only service-started process = 1 [verify] every number the walkthrough quotes matches the live index. ============================================================== The lab is ready.
That block is not decoration

Before saying "ready", the setup file re-runs every count this guide quotes, as a real query against the index it has just loaded, and stops if any of them disagrees. When you see that block, the guide and the data provably still agree with each other. If you change a number in this guide by hand, the setup file is what will catch you.

What it has just done for you

  • started Elasticsearch and Kibana in Docker,
  • created the throwaway account that both of them authenticate with,
  • installed the two index templates, so the field types are right,
  • imported all 420 documents,
  • created the two data views, so Discover can resolve a field list,
  • installed the detection rule and waited until that rule had actually fired.

Each of those is a way to end up with a lab that looks fine and quietly returns wrong answers. A data view with an empty index pattern, a skipped index template and a rule that never fires all produce a working-looking screen with zero results and no error message at all. The script refuses to leave you in that state.

Two things worth knowing

It is safe to run again

The script counts what is already loaded and skips the import, so you cannot end up with two copies of every event and a pile of wrong counts. If you want to start completely fresh, run setup-lab.cmd reset (or ./setup-lab.sh reset) — that removes the containers, the data volume and the data views, then rebuilds.

It refuses to touch anything that is not its own

Every container, volume and port is named after this folder. If something else is already answering on port 9200, or a container of the same name was created from a different copy of this folder, the script tells you so and stops — it will not delete a lab it did not start.

If you cannot use Docker

You can install the templates, import the two files and create the two data views by hand — the commands are printed in README.md and in guided-walkthrough.md. You then have no alerts, because there is no rule installed, so the next card has nothing to show. Everything after that works exactly the same way.

Start4

The browser has opened on the alerts page

do now

The setup file ends by opening Kibana in your browser. If no browser opened, or you closed the tab, go to http://localhost:5601 yourself.

If Kibana asks you to sign inusername lab_kibana password LabKibana001

These are throwaway lab credentials. They protect nothing and you may type them anywhere. The browser remembers you, so this is a one-time step.

Then confirm the two data views exist

Click the hamburger menu (☰) in the top-left corner, then Stack Management, then Data Views. You should see exactly two rows.

If they are not there, the setup file did not finish. Go back to the previous card rather than creating them by hand — if it stopped, it printed the reason.

Evidence5

The alert you were handed

do now

Before you search for anything, look at what the monitoring system already caught. This is the alert your instructor was given, and you are about to work out whether it was right.

Go to http://localhost:5601/app/security/alerts.

If the table is empty, it is the time picker and not a broken lab

An alert is stamped with the moment it was raised — minutes ago, because the rule runs every minute — and this page opens on Today, meaning from midnight. Click the time picker at the top right, switch to the Relative tab, and set it to 30 units Days. Some versions offer a ready-made Last 24 hours button there instead; that does the same job.

Open one of them

In the first column, called Actions, click the small expand icon — two arrows pointing outwards — on either row. A panel opens on the right. Read its Alert reason: it already names the program and its parent. For the raw log record underneath, click the Table tab at the top of the panel, and look at user.name and process.command_line there. That is also where the real event time is — the timestamp on the row itself is the time the rule ran, not the time the process started.

What to notice before you have run a single query

Two alerts, from one rule, on one host. That is itself a clue. The rule matches documents one-for-one, so it matched two — and the pair is the shape of the whole incident: something happened, and then the same thing happened again with more privilege. The next card shows you the rule that did it.

Evidence6

The rule that fired

reference

In the left-hand Security menu click Rules, then click the rule named Remote support agent installed or registered as a service.

Read that Query line. It is event.code: 4688 and (process.command_line: *--install* or process.command_line: *--service*) — any process creation, anywhere in the estate, whose command line carries an install or a service switch. Read that again: there is no host name in it. The rule asks about a technique, not about a machine.

Now count. Two processes all day carry those switches, and two alerts are on the Alerts page. Your own Query 2 in a few cards filters on the host instead of the command line, and returns the same two records — but neither query can see the scheduled task, and neither can see the beaconing at all, because that lives in a different data view.

One thing in rule.json still looks wrong on purpose

Its time window is 365 days, which is far wider than you would ever ship. That is because a rule's window is measured backwards from right now, and this lab's data is dated 22 September 2026 — so an ordinary five-minute window would match nothing and the rule would never fire, leaving the Alerts page permanently empty. In a real deployment you would use a narrow window. The logic of the rule is what you would ship: a technique, no host name, and a rule happy to raise two alerts rather than one summary line, because the two are the finding — the same binary, once as a user and once as SYSTEM.

This is all a detection rule is

One query, on a schedule, run for you. Everything from here on is you doing by hand, slowly and with no one watching, exactly what this rule does every minute. That is also why the rule has no threshold: without one, each of the two matching documents arrives as its own alert, so the alert stream shows you the pair rather than a bare count.

Search7

Open Discover and pick the auth data view

do now

Click the hamburger menu (☰) in the top-left corner, then Discover (on newer builds it sits under Analytics).

Then, at the top left, click the Data view dropdown and choose auth-*. That is where the logon, process and scheduled-task evidence lives. You will switch to network-* exactly once, in Query 5.

Why the data view matters more than it looks

Pick the wrong one and every query in the rest of this guide returns nothing, with no error message — the fields you are searching on simply do not exist there. The panel on the left is the fastest way to check you are in the right place: event.code, process.parent.name and service.name on the left means you are on auth-*.

Search8

Pin the time range, and the timezone trap

careful

Click the time picker at the top right. It says something like “Last 15 minutes”, which shows nothing, because this lab's data is from a fixed day in the past. Click the Absolute tab.

  • From → Sep 22, 2026 @ 00:00:00.000
  • To → Sep 22, 2026 @ 23:59:59.999

Click Apply, or press Enter.

You should now see the two date boxes filled in, and the histogram below showing the day's activity spread across it — a flat, noisy background with one obvious cluster near the right-hand end.

The one thing that will look “wrong”: Kibana prints times in your timezone

If you are in the Philippines the events show as the morning of the 23rd. In Europe they show as the small hours of the 23rd. Nothing is broken — the data is stored in UTC, and Kibana renders it in the browser's timezone. Two consequences, and both matter:

  1. Set the range wide enough to cover it. If you set the 22nd to the 22nd and everything is empty, widen it to the 23rd before you conclude anything else is wrong.
  2. Judge the gaps between events, not the absolute clock times. Every conclusion in this guide is about spacing and ordering, and those survive any timezone. Write down the gaps; write the times as your screen shows them.
The 30-second check

Run event.code: 4688. You should get 19 documents. If you get a much larger number, your range is still too wide. If you get zero, it is too narrow or the wrong data view. Those three outcomes tell you which of the two mistakes you have made, which is faster than staring at the screen.

Query 19

First: the scheduled task that was registered

do now

Start with the rarest event in the index — somebody scheduling something.

Type into the Discover search barevent.code: 4698
  • event.code: 4698 — keep only events of type “a scheduled task was created”.

Click Columns above the results and add @timestamp, host.name, service.name, user.name and process.name. Sort by @timestamp ascending.

What to notice

  • the user.name is SYSTEM, not a person. A task registered by the operating system's own account belongs to a program that installed itself, not to somebody setting up their own scheduled job.
  • the process.name is a program you are about to meet again in Query 2. Notice it now; do not conclude it is “the same” until you have seen it twice.
What suspicious looks like, versus benign

Suspicious: a task nobody admits to creating, registered by SYSTEM, for a program that was installed minutes ago. Benign: a task owned by the software team, registered by a named administrator, for a program that has been on the box for months.

Why start here

Persistence is what turns a one-off intrusion into a permanent one, and 4698 is the single best event to alert on for this technique. A program running is weak evidence — programs run all day. A task being created means somebody deliberately arranged for it to start again later, which is intent.

Query 110

Read that one record in full

do now

Click the small expand icon at the left of the row — the diagonal arrows. A panel opens under the row showing every field, with a Table tab and a JSON tab.

Two things to look at

  • message — the human-readable rendering of the same event in one sentence. Every record in this lab has one. Read it here; you will not be able to search it, and the next card explains why.
  • service.name — sitting in the middle of the field list on its own. That is the task name, and it is one of your best clues.
The habit worth forming here

Stop and read one document completely before you filter anything else. Columns are for scanning a hundred rows; a whole document is for understanding one. In a real investigation the difference between "that looks odd" and "that is definitely wrong" is almost always one document read end to end.

Detour11

Detour: check the mapping before you trust a field

optional

Two minutes that stop you trusting a result you should not. Go to http://localhost:5601/app/management/data/index_management, click the index auth-2026.09.22, then the Mappings tab, and type command_line into the Search fields box on that page.

Four things worth noticing across these two tabs

FieldTypeWhat that means for you
process.command_linekeywordStored whole and matched exactly. So the install switch you are about to read is a value you can rely on — and you can search for it precisely.
service.namekeywordAlso exact. The task name from Query 1 is an exact value, not a fuzzy match. It matters: the name is one of your best clues.
messagetextBroken into individual words for searching, so you cannot run an exact-match search against it. You have to read it, which is what the previous card was.
event.codelongA number, not a string. That is why every query in this guide says event.code: 4698 and never event.code: "4698".
Why this detour is not optional padding

The index template the setup file installed in card 3 is what decided all of this. Had it been skipped, Elasticsearch would have guessed these types from the first document it saw, and some of your queries would return zero results or the wrong results with no error message whatsoever. Checking a mapping before relying on a field is much faster than debugging a silent zero twenty minutes later — and it is the habit that separates people who can self-direct from people who cannot.

Query 212

The installation: every process on that server

core finding

This is the same query the shorter companion brief gives you as its single one-shot query. It is not the query the detection rule runs: the rule matches on the command line and never names a host. Both reach the same two records, which is the point of reading the two side by side.

Type into the Discover search barevent.code: 4688 and host.name: "sec-win-05"
  • event.code: 4688 — keep only “a new process has been created”.
  • host.name: "sec-win-05" — only on the server named in the alert.
  • and — both must be true.

Add @timestamp, process.name, process.parent.name, user.name and process.command_line as columns, sorted by @timestamp ascending.

Read both rows in time order. This is the technical core of the incident

  • the first row is a program being installed by an ordinary user. Its process.command_line contains an install switch and its parent is an ordinary desktop program. That is a person, at a keyboard, launching something.
  • the second row is the same program, now running as SYSTEM, with the Windows service controller as its parent. That combination means the program registered itself as a service: it starts at boot and runs whether or not anyone is logged in.
  • look at the program name itself. It is a commercially sold remote-support product — the kind your own help desk uses. That is not a detail to skip. It is the reason this attack is hard to block, and it belongs in your report.
Suspicious versus benign

Suspicious: a user installs a remote-support tool, and one minute later the same tool is running as a SYSTEM service. Benign: the IT team installs an approved tool from a named admin account during a change window, and it runs as a service the whole time — no sudden switch to SYSTEM right after a user-level install. The difference is not the tool. It is the privilege change.

Now click the expand icon on the first row and read the earlier of the two in full. You already met the message field in Query 1; this is where you read it for a process creation.

The sentence this card buys you

The change from a user to SYSTEM is the moment a tool stops being something someone launched and becomes something the machine runs on its own. Everything else in this incident — the task, the beacons — is a consequence of that one minute.

Query 213

Prove the dead end: what normal looks like

do now

Before you narrow further, check what the estate's normal looks like, so that the word “unusual” means something.

Replace the query withevent.code: 4688

Drop a couple of columns so the table is not cramped, then click the Field statistics tab next to Documents.

What to notice, and this is the whole point of the card

  • read the Documents count for the day and the Distinct values count for process.parent.name, and write both down. The day is a modest number of process creations, and almost all of them are ordinary people doing ordinary things.
  • the Distinct values count for process.parent.name is tiny, and one of those values is overwhelmingly the most common — that is the desktop, i.e. a person clicking something. Open its distribution chart and read the two bars.
  • the smaller bar is the Windows service controller. Write down how many records sit under it, then compare that with how many processes the alerted server started in the previous card.
  • if that number is one, then on this entire estate, for this entire day, exactly one process was started by the Windows service controller — and you already know which one it is, because it is on the server named in the alert.
How to turn “that looks odd” into “that is unique”

A finding that quotes a rate survives contact with a manager; a finding that quotes a feeling does not. “Out of every process started on this whole estate today, exactly one was started by the service controller, and it is the same program the alert named” is a sentence somebody can act on. The next card turns it into a query that says exactly that.

Query 314

The one process the service controller started

core finding
Type into the Discover search barevent.code: 4688 and process.parent.name: "services.exe"
  • keep only process creations whose parent is the Windows service controller;
  • note this query names no host — it is estate-wide. It is the direct follow-up to the Field statistics card, written out as a query.

Add @timestamp, host.name, process.name, user.name and process.command_line as columns.

The finding, in its strongest form

You no longer have “a user installed something and then it was running as SYSTEM”. You have “this is the only process on the entire estate today that anything started as a service”. A parent process is a fact about how something began, not an inference about what someone meant — which is why it is very hard to argue with.

Write this query into your report

Three of your five queries describe the attack chain. This one describes the baseline, and it is the one that makes the other three mean something. Evidence is not a list of hits; it is hits plus the comparison that shows why they are unusual.

Query 415

The logon that let the attacker in

core finding

Now the entry point — and the part students most often skip, because the tool is more interesting than the way it got there. Do not skip it.

Type into the Discover search barevent.code: 4624 and source.ip: "203.0.113.45"
  • event.code: 4624 — keep only “an account was successfully logged on”. Note this is a different code from the previous two: those were process creations, this is an actual session.
  • source.ip: "203.0.113.45" — the external address named in the alert. Type the value exactly, including the quotation marks.

Add @timestamp, user.name, host.name, host.ip, source.ip, source.port and logon.type as columns.

What to notice

  • the account on this logon is the same account that ran the installer in Query 2. That link is what makes this an intrusion rather than a coincidence, and it is the single most important cross-reference in the whole investigation.
  • host.ip is the server's own address. Copy it now — the next card filters on it.
  • logon.type is 3, a network logon: the session was used from somewhere else, not typed at that machine's keyboard.
  • the source.ip is outside your 10.0.4.0/24 range, so the session originated off the internet rather than from the office.
Why this card is not optional

It establishes that the machine was already under someone else's control before the tool appeared, and that matters twice over. First, the account must be treated as compromised — resetting it is part of the response, not an optional extra. Second, the tool is not the whole story: it is the second stage, and there is an earlier stage this lab does not contain. A report that only describes the remote-support tool has described the symptom and missed the entry.

Query 416

Read the logon record, and notice what the message does not say

do now

Click the expand icon on that row and read the record end to end.

Read the message field against the columns

The message says the logon was an “interactive session” from an external network. The logon.type column says 3, which is network, not interactive. A message that contradicts the structured field is itself a finding — somebody wrote a summary that does not match the telemetry underneath it.

Take the field, not the sentence

Always trust the structured field over the human-readable summary, because the summary is generated text and the field is the record. In a real investigation the gap between the two is often the most interesting thing on the screen: a tool that mislabels its own logon type, or a forwarder that fills in a field it should not know. Say so in your report.

Also check user.domain. It gives you the realm the account belongs to, and it is worth one line in your evidence: it tells you which directory the account lives in, which is what you need in order to reset it properly.

Query 517

What the server phoned home to

core finding

Now switch to the traffic data view and find where the installed tool talked to.

First, switch the Data view to network-*Data view (top left) -> network-*
Then type into the search barsource.ip: "10.0.4.13"
  • keep only traffic originating from the victim server — that is the host.ip value you copied in Query 4. If you read a different value there, use yours instead.
  • this is a deliberately blunt query: it filters on no protocol and no port, so it shows you everything that host sent. In this dataset that turns out to be only the beaconing — which is itself a finding.

Add @timestamp, url.domain, destination.ip, destination.port, network.bytes and source.port as columns, sorted by @timestamp ascending.

What to notice, and write all of it down

  • url.domain gives you the relay hostname. Compare it with the web destinations used elsewhere in this data: this one is not a vendor your estate normally talks to, and the name itself tells you which product was installed. Record it as an IOC.
  • destination.port is 443 — ordinary web TLS. That is exactly why this traffic does not stand out to a firewall, and it is worth a sentence in your report.
  • destination.ip is the address that name resolved to. Record it as an IOC.
  • network.bytes is small — a couple of kilobytes each. Say that in your report anyway. The volume is not the signal, and a reader who assumes “too small to matter” needs to be corrected by your writing rather than left to their own assumption. This is exactly the mistake people make with cryptominers.
  • source.port is the same on every row. Several sessions sharing one local port are one long-lived connection being re-established, not several separate visits.
Suspicious versus benign

Suspicious: small, perfectly periodic sessions from a server to a relay domain it has no business using, on the normal web port, over a single long-lived connection. Benign: sessions to recognised vendor domains, or relay traffic that is documented and approved in your estate.

This closes the loop

The process records show a tool was installed and made persistent. This shows it is actively talking to its operator's infrastructure, which is what makes the access live rather than abandoned — and it hands you the two things you can block and hunt on across the whole estate.

Query 518

See the pattern: zoom the range and let the chart say it

do now

Three rows in a table is fine. A chart makes the pattern obvious, and pattern is what you report.

Stay on the same Discover view. Open the time picker and narrow the range to 21:55:00 → 22:35:00 on 22 September 2026. Then set the interval dropdown next to the histogram to 5 minutes.

What to notice

  • the gaps between the bars are equal. Human-driven traffic clusters; this is a machine on a timer. Work out the gap and write the number down.
  • the whole thing occupies about ten minutes. There is no burst, no download, no scanning — the server is doing exactly one thing, quietly, on a schedule.
  • combine it with the source port: one destination, one local port, a fixed interval. Those three together are what turns a row of similar-looking records into a machine.

If you want the connection itself rather than the shape of it, click the expand icon on any of the three rows.

Why the picture is worth more than the sentence

“Some traffic to a vendor” and “traffic to a vendor on a perfect timer, from a server, with nothing else going on” are very different claims, and this chart is what lets you defend the second one. It is also the figure to include when you recommend blocking that destination estate-wide.

Query 519

Is that relay a stranger? Field statistics again

do now

You have called the relay domain unfamiliar. Prove it, rather than asserting it — and prove it against the whole index, not against the three rows you already have.

Clear the query box completely, so the whole of network-* is in scope, and click the Field statistics tab.

What to notice

  • read the chart bar by bar and sort the names into two piles: vendors your estate would obviously talk to on an ordinary day, and names it would not. The unfamiliar ones are your finding.
  • the chart labels itself “top 10”. That is itself a clue: there is at least one value behind it the chart is not showing you, so the distinct count is always the larger number.
  • read the host.name row on the same screen as well. A small distinct count there is what makes a single destination meaningful.
This is how you justify a word in your report

“The server talked to an IP address” means nothing on its own. “The server talked to a list of hostnames, all but one of which are approved vendors this estate uses daily, and the one exception is the relay from the previous card” is a finding — and this table is where that sentence comes from. Read the host.name row on the same screen as well: a small distinct count there is what makes a single destination meaningful.

The honest caveat, and it is a real one

There is no DNS lookup for the relay anywhere in this data. Every connection record names the domain directly in url.domain, and the 31 DNS records in the index cover 30 unrelated names. So you cannot show the moment the name was resolved, and you should not claim you can. Knowing what your data cannot tell you is part of the job — and “resolution of the relay is missing from the telemetry” is itself a detection gap worth one line in your recommendations.

Verify20

Verify your count, in JSON

do now

One exact number, checked properly, so you can state it without hedging in the report. Go to http://localhost:5601/app/dev_tools/console, click Clear this input, and type this — the path on the first line, the JSON body below it:

Into the Dev Tools editorGET auth-2026.09.22/_count { "query": { "bool": { "filter": [ { "term": { "event.code": 4688 } }, { "term": { "host.name": "sec-win-05" } } ] } } }

Click the ▶ button at the top right of the editor, or press Ctrl+Enter.

Now change the first line to GET auth-2026.09.22/_search, add "size": 1 and "sort": [{ "@timestamp": "asc" }] to the body, and run it again.

You should see one document — the earliest of the two, thanks to the sort — with the full command_line, the installing account, and the message field with the readable rendering of the same event.

Three screens now agree, and that is the point

The alerts page said 2. Your Discover query said 2. This says 2. Three independent routes to the same number is a far stronger sentence than one, and it is the difference between “I counted” and “I verified” in a report that somebody will act on.

The second thing this card taught you

The KQL you type in Discover and this JSON are two faces of the same query. That matters beyond the count: detection rules are written in the JSON form, so reading the earlier rule card and this one together tells you what a rule actually executes under the query box you have been typing in all afternoon.

Put it together21

Build the timeline — the heart of the report

oldest first6 min

You have proved several separate claims. An investigator, a manager or a court will not read separate claims — they will read one story in time order. Assemble it now, before you write a word of prose.

Do this

  1. Open the card at the end of this deck, and leave 2. Timeline empty.
  2. Copy the seven lines below, oldest at the top, into your own notes.
  3. Work out the gap after each one yourself and put it in brackets. The gaps are the finding; the timestamps are only the scaffolding.

Every timestamp below is printed on a screenshot earlier in this guide with a numbered circle on it, so you can check each one against your own screen. What the screenshots cannot show you is the seven of them together — and together they are the thing you are being asked to explain.

The seven events, interleaved from two different data views

  • 22:05:00.000
    Logon — mchen successfully authenticated on sec-win-05 (10.0.4.13), from 203.0.113.45 on port 51,744, logon.type: 3. auth-* The foothold, and the earliest thing that happened. Read this row twice. The log's own message calls it “Interactive session from an external network”, but logon.type: 3 means a network logon — nobody was at that keyboard. The field and the prose disagree, and the field is the one you can rely on.
  • 22:08:00.000  (+3 min)
    Process created — anydesk.exe, parent explorer.exe, by mchen, command line --silent --install. auth-* Three minutes after the logon, a person launched an installer with no dialog and no window. Parent explorer.exe means a human double-clicked something — this was a deliberate action, not a worm walking a network.
  • 22:09:00.000  (+1 min)
    Process created — anydesk.exe again, parent services.exe, by SYSTEM, command line --service. auth-* Sixty seconds later the same binary, started by the Service Control Manager, running as the machine itself. This is the most important line on the timeline. A move from a named user to SYSTEM is the moment a tool stops being something someone launched and becomes something the machine runs on its own.
  • 22:09:00.000  (same second)
    Scheduled task registered — AnyDesk Service, subject SYSTEM, running anydesk.exe --service. auth-* The same second as the line above, and the log says who did it: “Registered by the installed remote access agent.” The tool persisted itself — nobody registered anything by hand, and nobody declared it.
  • 22:11:00.000  (+2 min)
    First beacon — sec-win-05 opened a session to relay.anydesk.example (198.51.100.44) on port 443, 2,048 bytes, from source port 49,900. network-* First contact with the vendor's relay, two minutes after the tool became a service. Note that the source port is not ephemeral in any meaningful sense here: it is the same number on all three rows.
  • 22:16:00.000  (+5 min)
    Second beacon — same host, same domain, same address, same port, same source port 49,900, 1,920 bytes. network-* Nothing about this row on its own. Everything about it next to the other two.
  • 22:21:00.000  (+5 min)
    Third beacon — identical again, 2,176 bytes. network-* The last contact of the day. Three sessions, 6,144 bytes in total, and then the server went quiet.
16 min 00 stotal elapsed
180 · 60 · 0 · 120 sgaps before the beacons
300 s, 300 sthe beacon gaps, identical
0jitter between beacons
7rows, 2 data views
Read your own seven lines and you should see this shape

logon → install → service + task in the same second → beacon → beacon → beacon. Two things jump out, and only one of them is about volume.

First, the gaps change character half way through. Every gap up to the first beacon is a different length: 180 seconds, then 60, then zero — the service and the task land in the same second — then 120. That is a person working, and then a tool acting on itself: reading a screen, deciding, clicking. The last two gaps are identical to the second: 300, then 300. That is the boundary between the human and the machine, and it sits exactly where you would expect it to — the moment the software took over from the person who installed it.

Second, nothing about the beaconing is large. Three sessions and six kilobytes is not a data theft, and a volume-based control would never have looked at it. One account, one program, one host, and sixteen minutes.

Four things to get right on this timeline, and one to leave out

1. Read your times off your own screen, and say which timezone you read them in. Every log in this lab is stored in UTC, but Kibana prints clock times in your timezone. If your machine is not on UTC all seven of your timestamps will be shifted by your offset — and shifted consistently, so the ordering, the gaps and the five-minute pattern are all still exactly right. Put one line at the top of your timeline naming your timezone. An analyst who quietly mixes two timezones produces a timeline that contradicts itself and cannot be defended.

2. Do not use the alert's timestamp. That is the trap on this lab. The @timestamp on the Alerts page is the moment the rule ran, not the moment the events happened — the rule was installed today, so its alerts are stamped today, weeks after the intrusion. Every timestamp in your timeline must come from Discover, never from Alerts. If your first row says “October” you have copied the alert.

3. Do not invent an event before 22:05. It is very tempting to open the story with a line like “earlier — attacker steals mchen’s credentials” so it begins neatly. There is no evidence for it in this data. Leave the gap, and write “initial access not covered by available telemetry” as your first line. A timeline with a documented gap is trustworthy; one with a comfortable guess is not — and a report that guesses about initial access is a report that has quietly invented the most important fact in the case.

4. And do not put the last beacon's absence on the timeline either. The data stops at 22:21 because the generator stops. You do not know whether the operator kept control afterwards, and nothing in the evidence tells you. Saying “the server went quiet” is an observation; saying “the attacker went away” is a conclusion you have not earned.

5. Leave the noise out. The other 270 authentication events and 145 network events belong to the three healthy machines and are not part of this story. A timeline should contain only the events that advance it; context belongs in a different section.

Why the five-minute repeat is the strongest thing you have

Nobody keeps time like that. A person checking in produces gaps that wander; a program produces gaps that are exactly as long as they said they would be. Two consecutive gaps of 300 seconds with zero jitter is a timer, and a timer is evidence you can hand to a detection engineer who wants to write a rule against it — which is precisely what the detection rule in this lab does with the other half of the chain.

Say so in those words in your report. It turns six observations into a described technique, and a described technique is worth more than a list of timestamps.

The one-line version, ready to lift to the top of your report

This is a model answer and it is here on purpose: this card is where you learn what a finished timeline should sound like. Every figure in it is one you can reproduce on screen. Copy the structure, not the words — your own summary must be written in your own words, and the fields on the last card stay blank until you write them.

Summary lineOn 22 September 2026 between 22:05 and 22:21 UTC the account mchen authenticated to sec-win-05 (10.0.4.13) from the external address 203.0.113.45 with a network logon, and three minutes later installed the remote support agent anydesk.exe under that account. Sixty seconds after that the same binary was running as SYSTEM with services.exe as its parent, and in the same second the agent registered its own scheduled task, AnyDesk Service. The host then contacted the relay relay.anydesk.example (198.51.100.44:443) three times at exactly five-minute intervals - 2048, 1920 and 2176 bytes from the same source port 49900 - and then went quiet. Total elapsed time sixteen minutes. Assessed as a TRUE POSITIVE: remote monitoring and management abuse, establishing durable remote access to a server. Initial access is not covered by the available telemetry.
Next

Timeline done. Now write the report around it — the last card has the sections, and they are still empty.

Deliverable22

Write the report, then prove it

do now

Nobody reads your screen. This card is the deliverable — it is the thing you hand in, and it is the only place in the guide you type. It has two parts and both go into your submission: Part one is your written report, Part two is the set of figures you checked off your own screen as you went. Neither part has an answer printed next to it. Fill both in, then press EXPORT MY SUBMISSION at the bottom: a finished PDF report lands in your Downloads folder with your name and batch number on the front of it.

Do this yourself, and do it now

If you cannot fill a line in without going back to Kibana, you have not finished the investigation — which is exactly the point. These fields are deliberately empty and stay that way until you type. Nothing here is marked against a model answer; it is marked on whether you found these things.

Both of these are printed at the top of the exported PDF and go into the file name, so the submission is identifiable without you having to say who you are in the report itself. Leave either one blank and the file still exports — it just says [not answered] where your name should be, which is a good reason not to leave them blank.

Part one — your report

1. Summary

What happened

two or three sentences a manager could follow, and no jargon in the first sentence

2. Timeline

When

the seven rows from card 21, in that order, with the gap after each one — and every timestamp checked off your own screen as you went

3. Evidence

How you know

each query you ran, the number it returned, and what that number proved. The number matters as much as the reasoning

4. Verdict

True positive or false positive

state it plainly in the first line, then the whole chain in one paragraph

5. Recommendations

What should happen next

concrete actions in the order you would carry them out. Remember that the account is compromised even though the tool is legitimate — the tool was the second stage, so the entry point still needs an answer

Every line below is a number you should be able to point at on your own screen. These travel with your report, so a figure that contradicts your writing gives you away — if Part one and Part two disagree, one of them is wrong, and you want to know which before you hand it in.

Finish23

Tear the lab down

do now

When you are finished — or when the next cohort needs the machine.

Run one of theseWindows teardown.cmd macOS/Linux ./teardown.sh

It prints the exact list of what it is about to remove, then asks you to confirm. Read the list, then answer Y.

What it prints before it deletes anything The following will be REMOVED. Nothing else will be touched. container rmm-tool-abuse-001-elasticsearch container rmm-tool-abuse-001-kibana volume rmm-tool-abuse-001_esdata file .../docker-compose.yml folder .../elklab-rmm-tool-abuse-001 Deliberately KEPT, always: - all Docker images, so the next setup is fast and offline - every other container, volume and image on this machine - the files in this folder (ndjson, templates, rule.json, the scripts)
Why it is safe on a shared machine

Every name it touches is derived from this folder's name using the same expression the setup file used, so it cannot name an object belonging to another scenario lab. If the folder has been copied and another copy already owns a container of the same name, the setup file stops and tells you rather than destroying it — and so does the teardown, which only reports what it actually removed and warns about anything left behind.

To stop the lab but keep the data, run docker compose -f docker-compose.yml down instead. Next time, the setup file picks the data back up and finishes in seconds.

Reference≡

If something goes wrong

reference

Almost every problem in this lab has one of four causes: Docker, the time range, the data view, or the setup script stopped. Find yours here before you start guessing.

What you seeWhat it meansWhat to do
docker was not found, or the engine is not respondingDocker Desktop is not installed, not started, or still startingStart Docker and wait until it says the engine is running, then run the setup file again
something else is already using port 9200A different Elasticsearch is answering there, and the script will not touch a cluster it did not startStop the other stack (find it with docker ps), or run teardown from the folder that owns it
a container called rmm-tool-abuse-001-elasticsearch already exists … created from a different folderThe folder was copied or moved, so an earlier copy owns the containerThe script shows you the details and deletes nothing. Follow the two docker commands it prints, or run teardown from the original folder
Elasticsearch did not become ready in timeUsually not enough memory for DockerClose other applications, or give Docker Desktop more memory, then run again
the auth index holds N documents but this lab ships 272A partial import, from something interruptedRun setup-lab.cmd reset (or ./setup-lab.sh reset) to rebuild the data exactly as shipped
The alerts page is empty but the setup file said the rule firedThe alerts page has its own time picker and opened on Today, while the alerts were raised minutes ago — or you crossed midnightSet the alerts time picker to a Relative range of 30 days
Discover shows “No results match your search criteria”Almost always the time range, not the queryWiden the range to two whole days, then narrow again. A too-narrow range hides everything, silently
Discover shows zero fields in the sidebarThe data view’s index pattern matches no indexsetup-lab.cmd reset — it rebuilds the data views
Query 1 returns 19 but a later query returns nothingYou are on the wrong data view for that queryauth-* for all the account and process queries; network-* only for the traffic query
Your results are on the 23rd, not the 22ndThat is your timezone, not a broken labNothing to fix — but widen the range to cover both days, and quote the gaps between events rather than the absolute times
A value you copied from one screen does not match anotherThe two screens keep separate time pickersSet both to cover the period you are reading before you compare anything
A query returns nothing and you are sure the field existsCapitalisation. Every field here is an exact keywordCopy the value out of the results rather than retyping it
Kibana asks for a login you do not haveYou typed the wrong lab accountlab_kibana / LabKibana001 — the same two the setup file printed
The 30-second checklist

Data view right? → Time range says a date, not “Last 15 minutes”? → Query text in the bar? → The number beside Documents matches the number this guide quotes? If all four are true and something still looks wrong, press F5, set the range again, and re-run the queries from the top. If event.code: 4688 does not return 19, your time range is still wrong; if it does, the problem is in the query text rather than in the dates.
